title: Ask for the right kind of help

---
title: Ask for the right kind of help
summary: Compare hints, worked examples and independent attempts to select assistance that develops understanding.
language: science
shape: 5e
unit: learning-effectively-with-ai
order: 11
voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 }
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8241
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8241/index.html
  readySelector: "#gpanel"
  layout: full
explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "Choose how much help to request"
  say: "Good assistance depends on what you are trying to learn."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "Try a learning challenge independently first." }
    - wait: 1000
    - caption: { text: "Request a hint, or inspect a worked example when needed." }
    - wait: 1000
    - caption: { text: "Then try a new question to test your own understanding." }
    - wait: 1000
---
Earlier you saw that AI writes by predicting likely next words, one at a time. That makes it fast at producing finished answers, but a finished answer can skip the thinking you came to practise. In the previous unit, you learned how to ask and follow up. Now consider **what kind of help actually develops your understanding**. AI might explain, question, offer hints, provide feedback or complete the task. The best choice depends on what you need to learn.

## Engage: what kind of help?

```step
stage: predict
check:
  type: predict
  q: "You are learning to add unlike fractions. Which assistance is most likely to let you practise the method yourself?"
  options: ["Copy a finished answer immediately", "Ask for one hint, then attempt the next step", "Avoid checking errors"]
  actual: "A hint can support practice while leaving the next step to the learner, though sometimes a worked example is appropriate."
```

## Explore: try different amounts of help

```step
stage: run
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#explore", height: 690 }
check: { type: board, text: "Complete an independent transfer attempt after inspecting the available assistance.", when: "t >= 1" }
```

The board contains **prepared hints and worked examples**, not a live AI tutor. Begin with a maths or science challenge, **write an attempt**, then ask for a hint if you need one. When you are ready, press **Try a new question** and attempt it without looking back. Say how sure you are, record it, then compare with the model answer. Try it once with a hint and once with the worked example: which left more of the thinking to you? A worked example is not inherently bad; it may be useful when you are new to the method or genuinely stuck.

## Explain: help or replacement?

```step
stage: investigate
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "On the board, you asked for one hint and then wrote the rest yourself. Your friend pressed Show worked example straight away. Who did more of the thinking?"
      options: ["You: the hint left the next steps to you", "Your friend: the worked example has more steps in it", "The same: you both saw the method"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "More steps on the screen isn't more thinking by your friend.", "Seeing a method isn't the same as working it out."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "After using the worked example for 1/2 + 1/4, which result is the best evidence you learned the method?"
      options: ["You get the new question, 1/3 + 1/6, right without looking back", "You understood the worked example while reading it", "You chose high confidence"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Understanding while reading can feel like learning. A new question tests it.", "Confidence is a guess. The model answer checks it."]
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can explain when hints, feedback or worked examples support my learning." }
```

### Choose

What were you able to attempt before asking for help?

### Compare

Which type of assistance was useful, and why did it suit your current knowledge?

### Transfer

Could you complete a related task without copying the example? What still needs practice?

## Elaborate: design a helpful request

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
check: { type: reflect, text: "I completed and explained an independent application of this lesson." }
```

Choose something you are currently learning. Write three possible AI requests: **a hint**, **feedback on your attempt** and **a worked example**. Decide when each might be useful. Then write a fourth request that asks for a new question so you can test whether you learned the skill.

## Evaluate: decide independently

```step
stage: info
check:
  type: match
  q: "You are learning to add fractions. Match each moment to the help that suits it best."
  pairs:
    - ["You have never seen the method and don't know where to start", "A worked example, then a new question to try alone"]
    - ["You are halfway through and stuck on one step", "One hint, then try the next step yourself"]
    - ["You have finished and want to know if it is right", "Feedback on your attempt"]
    - ["You think you have got it", "A new question to try without help"]
  explain: "The right help depends on where you are. A worked example suits the very start; a hint suits being stuck; feedback suits a finished try; a new question shows whether you can do it alone."
```

Without the board, explain the difference between *completing a task* and *learning to complete that kind of task*. Include one example of appropriate assistance.

## Learning with AI: keep the learner active

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can say which kind of help I need right now, and why." }
```

Before asking AI for help, consider what you already know and what you need to practise. A useful assistant may give a question or feedback rather than the answer. But requiring struggle without support is not the goal either. Adjust the assistance as your understanding changes.

## Optional: try it with an AI tool

```step
stage: info
tier: typical
prompt:
  title: "Hint-first help"
  text: |
    I'm learning [what you are learning]. Here is my attempt so far: [paste or describe it].
    Please don't give me the answer. Give me one hint for my next step, then wait for me to try.
    If I'm still stuck after two hints, show me a worked example of a similar question, not mine.
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared the AI's reply with the board's hints, and said whether it left the next step to me." }
```

Use the prompt below on something you are learning. Then compare the reply with the board: did it give one hint and leave the next step to you, or hand you the answer? If it gave the answer, say so and ask again.

**No AI tool?** Ask a partner to be the tutor and follow the same prompt.

```teacher
summary: Choose among hints, worked examples and independent practice based on
  the learning goal.
time: 30
goals:
  - I can select assistance that leaves appropriate thinking for me to practise.
  - I can check learning by completing a related task independently.
before: >
  The board uses scripted hints and worked examples rather than live AI. Do not
  imply that hints are always preferable: worked examples can reduce
  unproductive confusion for novices.

  The core board is offline and requires no AI account. If your school allows
  it, you can demonstrate a hint-first request in a school-approved assistant
  yourself.

  The optional AI-tool step (typical width) is never needed to finish, and every
  check can be done without AI. Students use an AI tool only if the school
  allows it and you say so; check the tool's terms first, since many require
  users to be 13 or older. The step gives a no-AI version (a partner or a
  table).
running:
  - "Engage: ask which help leaves the next step to the learner before anyone
    opens the board."
  - "Explore: students do the challenge twice, once with a hint and once with
    the worked example, and compare."
  - "Explain: ask who did the thinking in each run."
struggle: Students may think every finished example is harmful, or that looking
  at an answer proves learning.
stuck:
  - see: A student goes straight to the worked example every time.
    ask: What could you try before looking? Which part are you stuck on?
    fix: Ask for one hint, write the next step, then decide if you need more.
support: "Model one run aloud: attempt, one hint, attempt, new question."
stretch: Apply the decision to a different subject or to performance rather than
  learning mode.
leads: Next, examine why useful-looking AI responses still require verification.
exit:
  q: You used the worked example. How can you tell whether you learned the method?
  a: Try a new question without looking back. If you can do it, the example helped
    you learn; if not, you followed it without learning it yet.
explain: >
  These are prepared cases and feedback, not outputs of an AI language model.

  The learning objective is transferable judgement, not a vendor-specific
  technique.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Is a worked example a shortcut or a good way to learn?
    prompts:
      - What did you do after seeing the example?
      - When would a hint be better?
    notes: It depends on when and how it is used. A worked example studied then
      followed by your own attempt can help a beginner; copying it is a
      shortcut.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: discussion
      title: Hint, example or try alone?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Stand at one of three corners: hint, worked example, try alone, for
        'learning to add 1/2 + 1/3'. Explain your corner, then move if you would
        choose differently for a topic you already know.
      notes: Movement shows that the right help depends on what you already know.
    - at: run
      kind: activity
      title: Three amounts of help
      minutes: 6
      do: >
        Pairs solve 1/2 + 1/4: one with a single written hint, one with a worked
        example to study then cover, one alone. Each then tries 1/3 + 1/6 with
        nothing.
      notes: The second question is the evidence. Compare who could do it without
        help.
    - at: make
      kind: activity
      title: Ask for the right help
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Write a request for help that asks for one hint, not the answer, on
        something you are learning. Read it to a partner, who checks it keeps
        you doing the thinking.
      notes: Check each request names the help type and leaves the work to the
        student.
```
